title: Income risk rose especially sharply at the top, increasing saving and wealth inequality in the model
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35664; digitized U.S. tax returns from 1969-2019 and a life-cycle model
geography: United States; tax-return income distribution, permanent and transitory income risk, saving, wealth, and financial distress

risk_trend.value: permanent income risk increased across the distribution and nearly 70% among the top 5%

distress.value: large negative income shocks strongly predicted financial distress even among top earners

saving_model.value: higher risk at the top increased saving and wealth inequality in the life-cycle model

rate_model.value: the modeled risk-free-rate effect was a 0.7 percentage-point reduction

observations.method: The authors use newly digitized U.S. tax returns to separate permanent and transitory income risk from 1969 to 2019, relate negative shocks to financial distress, and use a quantitative life-cycle model to study saving, wealth inequality, and the risk-free rate.
observations.uncertainty: The tax records do not explain each saving decision, asset destination, firm response, borrower rate, housing-price effect, or political response. The 0.7 percentage-point rate result is model-based and is not a rate change for every household or loan.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households across the income distribution, especially the top 5%; risk, assets, debt, liquidity, occupation, business ownership, and ability to wait vary within the top group and across lower-income households.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher saving can support investment, resilience, and future consumption rather than only reduce demand or widen inequality. A lower modeled risk-free rate can help some borrowers while asset-price increases or credit standards hurt others; the study does not identify the pass-through.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 35664

boundary: This record adds a distributional-finance finding: risk, saving, wealth, credit conditions, and household security can move on different levels and clocks. It does not establish that top-income saving caused any particular lower-income household's rent, loan rate, wage, distress, or political response.
